meta.title: Per-tenant API rate limiting
meta.ask: Approve a Redis-backed token bucket per tenant that fails open to local buckets, and the four-stage rollout.

summary: Give every tenant a fair share of the public API. The gateway checks a token bucket per tenant in Redis. Tenants over their limit get 429 with Retry-After; if Redis is unavailable, the gateway falls back to local buckets so traffic keeps flowing.

problem.statement: One tenant's traffic spike can exhaust the shared Orders service. In Q2 this caused 6 incidents where every tenant saw timeouts. The only protection today is a global cap at the load balancer, which throttles all tenants equally, including the ones behaving well.

metrics.label: Other tenants' p99 during a burst

requirements.text: Reject requests over a tenant's limit within 1 second of the limit being exceeded.
Rejected requests return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers.
The limiter adds at most 2 ms to gateway p99 latency.
A limiter or Redis failure never blocks traffic; on-call is alerted within 5 minutes.
Per-tenant limits change without a deploy.

nonGoals: Monthly quotas and billing (owned by the billing team)
Blocking abusive IPs (handled by the WAF)

architecture.before: Today every request goes straight from the gateway to Orders. Nothing distinguishes one tenant from another until the load balancer's global cap trips.
architecture.after: A limiter inside the gateway checks each tenant's bucket in Redis before forwarding. Limits come from hot-reloaded config (R-5). If Redis can't answer in time, a local bucket takes over (R-4).

steps.text: Tenant acme sends POST /orders with its API key.
The gateway resolves the tenant from the key and asks the limiter for one token.
One atomic Lua script in Redis refills the bucket by elapsed time and takes a token. One round trip, about 0.4 ms at p50.
Token granted. 11 of 20 tokens left in acme's burst allowance.
The request is forwarded to Orders with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 11.
acme is bursting: its 21st request inside one second.
The gateway asks the limiter for a token.
The bucket is empty. Refill rate is 20 tokens per second.
Denied. Redis reports the next token arrives in 50 ms.
The client gets 429 with Retry-After: 1. The request never reaches Orders, so other tenants are untouched.
The gateway asks the limiter for a token.
Redis doesn't answer within the 5 ms budget. The circuit breaker opens after 20 consecutive timeouts.
The limiter fails open to an in-process bucket sized at the tenant limit divided by 8 replicas. Accuracy drops; availability holds.
The request is served. An alert fires if more than 1% of traffic uses the fallback for 5 minutes.

options.name: Fixed window counter
notes: Up to 2× the limit across a window boundary
options.verdict: Rejected: boundary bursts are exactly the noisy-neighbor pattern we're fixing.

options.name: Sliding window log
notes: One entry per request; the largest tenant needs ~40 MB
options.verdict: Rejected: exact, but memory grows with traffic and it costs 3 round trips.

options.name: Token bucket (GCRA)
options.verdict: Chosen: one atomic call, constant memory, and burst size is a tunable we can give sales.

risks.title: Redis latency spikes slow every request
risks.mitigation: 5 ms timeout per call, circuit breaker, fail open to local buckets (R-4).

risks.title: Tenants exceed limits during a Redis outage
risks.mitigation: Local bucket is limit ÷ replicas; alert when fallback traffic passes 1%.

risks.title: A misconfigured limit throttles a large customer
risks.mitigation: Shadow mode first; audit log on limit changes; per-tenant override without deploy.

risks.title: Clock skew between gateway replicas
risks.mitigation: The Lua script reads time from Redis TIME, not the gateway clock.

risks.title: The largest tenant creates a hot key on one shard
risks.mitigation: Per-shard CPU alert; split the tenant's bucket across 4 keys if it trips.

rollout.name: Shadow mode
rollout.detail: Decide every request and log would-be 429s. Enforce nothing.

rollout.name: 5% of tenants
rollout.detail: Internal tenants plus customers who opted in.

rollout.name: 50% of tenants
rollout.detail: Random half, excluding the top 10 tenants by volume.
rollout.gate: No tickets citing 429s from tenants under their limit

rollout.name: All tenants
rollout.detail: Top 10 tenants join last, each with a named contact.

questions.text: Should internal service accounts bypass the limiter, or get their own higher limits?
Do we show each tenant its limits in the developer dashboard at launch, or in a follow-up?
Should free-tier tenants fail closed instead of open during a Redis outage?
